title: The Real How Jack the Ripper Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a time-travel bit at the Britannia Pub and the Annie Chapman crime scene, then cover the canonical Jack the Ripper murders of 1888 in London's Whitechapel (Polly Nichols, Annie Chapman, Elizabeth Stride, Catherine Eddowes, Mary Jane Kelly), the grim East End backdrop, the Squibby mob incident, the modus operandi and profile (including the FBI's John Douglas), the Dear Boss and From Hell letters, the case's historians and suspects (Robert Mann, Walter Sickert and Patricia Cornwell's book, Michael Ostrog, Montague Druitt, Aaron Kosminski, Severin Klosowski/George Chapman), and the case's legacy. Recorded as a Halloween episode.

segments.title: Time-travel opening at the Annie Chapman crime scene
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open in a playful time-travel bit outside the Britannia Pub, visiting the scene where Annie Chapman was killed, and Josh points out her wounds and the arched-leg posture that becomes a Ripper signature.

segments.title: The canonical murders and the Whitechapel backdrop
segments.summary: The hosts list the five canonical murders from August to November 1888 and mention possible earlier victim Martha Tabram. They describe East End poverty, alcoholism, disease, opium, and casual prostitution, and George Bernard Shaw's remark that the murders exposed London's living conditions.

segments.title: The victims and the Squibby mob
segments.summary: The hosts profile the victims Polly Nichols, Elizabeth Stride, and Catherine Eddowes, noting their drinking and casual prostitution, and the stories of their lives. They then recount how police chasing a tattooed man named Squibby set off a mob that believed he was the Ripper.

segments.title: Mary Jane Kelly's crime scene and early crime photography
segments.summary: The hosts visit the Miller's Court scene of Mary Jane Kelly's murder, the last canonical killing, which they describe as the most severe mutilation and involving an axe. They discuss the crime scene photograph, often cited as one of the first, and the body parts left at the scene.

segments.title: Modus operandi, offender profile, and the Ripper letters
segments.summary: The hosts describe the killer's modus operandi: weekend and early-morning attacks, strangulation followed by throat-cutting from left to right, and signs of anatomical knowledge. They cover the police theory of a madman, the 2006 Scotland Yard description, the FBI profile by John Douglas, and the Dear Boss letter, which gave the name Jack the Ripper and was followed by a related ear mutilation.

segments.title: Forgery theories, multiple killers, and lost evidence
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Andrew Cook's claim that reporter Frederick Best forged the Dear Boss letter to boost newspaper sales, Percy Clark's comment that one man may have been responsible for three murders, and why the case is hard to solve because evidence was lost, taken as souvenirs, or destroyed.

segments.title: Suspects: Robert Mann, Walter Sickert, and Patricia Cornwell
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the more than 100 named suspects, the recent Robert Mann identification by historian Russell Edwards, Mann's role as a morgue attendant and why his alibi is doubted, and Patricia Cornwell's book Case Closed naming painter Walter Sickert, including her mitochondrial DNA evidence and the criticism of it.

segments.title: Police suspects, Klosowski, and the Ripper legacy
segments.summary: The hosts cover other suspects, including Lewis Carroll, Prince Albert Victor, and the Freemasons, and the three suspects named by Neville Macnaghten (Ostrog, Druitt, Kosminski). They favor George Chapman (Severin Klosowski), a convicted poisoner, and close with the case's legacy, including early forensic methods, the press-serial killer relationship, and pop culture.

segments.title: Halloween sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close with a Halloween greeting, a note about the casebook.org resource, and an invitation to email suspect ideas to the show.
